## Page 1: SalePrologo

### Full · `saleprologo.mp3` · 244 words

> To whoever breaks these seals.
>
> If you are reading this, I am dead, and someone has respected my last wishes: I am surprised, and I thank you. This file was begun by my father, Silas Pell, your family's notary for forty years, and I kept it for another thirty. Inside are letters, police reports, cuttings from the gazette, a will and a handwriting expert's report: everything two honest notaries could gather about a man who, according to the register of births, was never born.
>
> Read the documents in the order I have put them, and skip none. And forgive my hand in the last pages: for some years now I have written badly, and some mornings I hardly recognise my own handwriting.
>
> At ten in the morning, in the village cemetery, in the presence of the heirs, the parish priest and the undersigned, the remains of the deceased were laid to rest, closed in the coffin the evening before by the carpenter and not reopened since, by his express wish. Overcast sky. Some twenty people present, nearly all out of curiosity.
>
> It is noted, for thoroughness, that at the far end of the cemetery, by the gate, stood a man whom none of those present could name: short of stature, in a black coat too large for him. During the blessing the man was laughing. When the undersigned approached to ask for his particulars, the gate was open and he was gone.

## Page 2: SaleG1Intro

### Full · `saleg1intro.mp3` · 277 words

> The heirs gathered in the estate library the day after the burial, at five in the afternoon. The curtains were drawn, as always in that house; the fire was out, and no one asked for it to be lit. The undersigned broke the seals in the presence of all and read the document aloud, written in the deceased's own hand two years ago.
>
> The estate, with the laboratory, the instruments, the animals and the debts, goes in equal shares to the children. The Journal goes to whoever can read it. So far, nothing strange.
>
> There follows a clause, which the undersigned had to read twice at the request of those present: *"Should I disappear without explanation, or die in circumstances my notary judges doubtful, all the rest of my property, the money in the bank, the shares and the key to the study on the alley, shall go to my friend Mr. Umber, who will know how to put it to good use."*
>
> None of those present knows a Mr. Umber. No one knew the deceased had a friend. No one, to tell the truth, knew the estate had a study on the alley.
>
> The undersigned notes that the deceased died in his bed, of a fever, attended by the village doctor: the circumstances are not doubtful. The undersigned will nonetheless hand nothing over to anyone until this Mr. Umber presents himself at his office, in person and in broad daylight.
>
> Before taking his leave, the undersigned gave each of the heirs a page of the Journal, torn out and sealed, with their name written on it by the deceased. They too were in the will.

## Page 3: SaleG2Intro

### Full · `saleg2intro.mp3` · 240 words

> My father died two years ago, pen in hand, halfway through a deed of sale. He left me his practice, his clients, a locked cupboard whose key I have never found, and this file, which I should never have reopened.
>
> In twenty-five years the village has become a town. The half-timbered houses have fallen one after another, and in their place have grown houses of grey stone, all alike, with gas lamps outside the door. The railway has come, and with the railway the soot. Of the old man nothing more has been heard: in law he died in 1861, and no one has any wish to reopen the matter.
>
> The sightings of Mr. Umber, on the other hand, have never stopped. A little man in a black coat, not a day older, who pays with cheques signed by respectable people and laughs at the end of the street. Today the heirs of the estate are the old man's grandchildren. None of them has ever seen the phials of salt, and all of them know where they are.
>
> They grew up on the stories, the way one grows up on bread: the grandfather who was not dead, the coffin full of stones, the door with no handle. At school their classmates dared each other to touch the estate's gate. Now the classmates are lawyers, doctors, town councillors, and cross to the other side of the street.

## Page 4: SaleG3Intro

### Full · `saleg3intro.mp3` · 234 words

> The town has electric light, a tramway and two newspapers that hate each other: a liberal one, which blames everything on the rich, and a conservative one, which blames everything on the poor. On one thing they agree: Mr. Umber sells copies. On the hill, beside the asylum, an Institute of science has risen, all glass and brass, and its professors write to the papers that the estate's salt is a country superstition.
>
> They are wrong, but not entirely. In recent years some young people of the town bought the new salt from Lomax, for a bet or out of despair, and drank it. The new salt works: the other one goes out, as always. But in the morning it does not come back. Two of them are in the asylum, laughing day and night; the third has not been seen since. I knew him. He was my neighbour's son, and always raised his hat to me.
>
> As for me, I am fifty-six, with a cough the doctors cannot cure. I sleep little, I write badly, I wear gloves even in summer because of an eczema on my hands. The practice runs on by force of habit, with the old clerk treating me like a sick son. I have decided to keep this file in order to the end. Whoever reads it after me will judge whether it was worth it.
